results.summary_before: This is a bit-serial implementation of the SIMON-128 lightweight block cipher, trading throughput for a compact area dominated by flip-flops and multiplexers. A 2-bit control word on ui[7:6] selects idle, plaintext load, key load, or encrypt, with serial data entering on ui[0] and ciphertext emerging on uo[0] over 128 consecutive clock cycles, flagged by a valid bit on uo[7]. The design is verified through a testbench containing example test vectors, and no external hardware is required. The documentation notes a limitation in the key-loading process and includes a debug bit to verify key register loading.

results.summary_before: Glyph Mode is a standalone VGA demo submitted for the VGA Demoscene competition. It generates a display and allows palette selection via two input pins, choosing between green, red, blue, or pride color schemes. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA monitor, and operates at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, including palette changes, and it also functions at higher clock speeds.

results.summary_before: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.

results.summary_before: This design drives an animation on a SparkFun RGB LED 8x8 matrix backpack using an SPI master interface. The animation features overlapping green and blue waves with a moving white diagonal, and some seven-segment wires are repurposed for a sanity check animation. It requires an external RGB LED matrix backpack and operates with a clock up to 12.5 kHz. The design includes an asynchronous reset synchronized to the clock.

results.summary_before: This chip performs conversions and comparisons between binary-encoded ternary and unary-encoded ternary, with both machine-readable and human-readable outputs. It supports four operation modes selected by opcodes, and outputs results either on a 7-segment display or as binary signals. The design is implemented using mixed radix circuit synthesis (MRCS) and Wokwi, and it can be tested by setting the mode and input pins to verify the conversion or comparison. No external hardware is required.
